lesson.title: A Continent Catches Fire: The Great Awakening
lesson.summary: A wave of emotional religious revivals swept the American colonies in the 1730s and 1740s, challenging established churches and giving colonists their first shared cultural experience across regional lines.
lesson.body:
By the early 1700s, many ministers worried that the religious intensity of the first Puritan generations had faded. In Massachusetts Bay Colony, where the founders had crossed the Atlantic to build a godly community, church membership was declining and worship had become, in the eyes of critics, routine and unfeeling. Meanwhile the Middle Colonies, home to Quakers, Presbyterians, Lutherans, Dutch Reformed congregations, and many others, already contained a patchwork of faiths with no single established church to enforce conformity. This mix of spiritual anxiety in New England and religious diversity in the Middle Colonies created fertile ground for something new.

That something was the Great Awakening, a series of revivals that spread through the colonies roughly between the 1730s and the 1740s. Revival preachers rejected the idea that faith was mainly a matter of correct doctrine learned from an educated minister. Instead they preached that true religion required a personal, often emotional experience of conversion, a moment when an individual truly felt their own sinfulness and God's grace. Sermons grew dramatic and vivid, congregations wept and cried out, and revival meetings sometimes drew crowds far larger than any single church could hold.

No single figure did more to spread the movement than George Whitefield, an English evangelist who made several preaching tours of the colonies beginning in 1739. Whitefield preached outdoors to enormous crowds from Georgia to New England, using a powerful voice and theatrical delivery that reportedly moved even skeptics like Benjamin Franklin, who admired Whitefield's speaking even without sharing his theology. Because Whitefield and other traveling preachers moved between colonies that otherwise had little contact with one another, the Great Awakening became one of the first experiences shared broadly across British North America, helping colonists imagine themselves as part of something larger than their individual colony.

The revivals split congregations and communities into New Lights, who supported the emotional new style of preaching, and Old Lights, who defended traditional, more formal worship led by educated clergy. This split weakened the authority of established churches, since New Light believers often left old congregations to form new ones or joined growing denominations like the Baptists and later the Methodists. It also encouraged ordinary people to question inherited authority more broadly, since the revivals suggested that a plowman's spiritual insight might matter as much as a Harvard educated minister's training.

Historians still debate exactly how directly the Great Awakening connects to the political revolution that followed decades later, but the connections are hard to ignore. The revivals normalized public gatherings that questioned established authority, encouraged religious pluralism that made single established churches harder to defend, and gave colonists practice imagining collective action across colonial borders. The next major figure in this story, the Massachusetts minister Jonathan Edwards, would become both the intellectual anchor of the Awakening's theology and the author of its most famous sermon.
